To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
participation in colorectal screening was associated with a decrease in smoking, an increase in fruit and vegetable consumption, and an increase in vigorous physical activity.
participation in faecal occult blood screening was associated with a decreased likelihood of smoking and an increased likelihood of meeting the fruit and vegetable consumption recommendations.
the odds of smoking were 0.45 (95% CI:0.29– 0.68) lower, and the odds of meeting fruit and vegetable consumption were 1.70 (95% CI :1.14– 2.55) higher in FOBT participants
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of participation in population-based colorectal cancer screening on lifestyle behaviours.
the effect of participation in a population-based colorectal cancer screening (CRCs) programme on multiple lifestyle behaviours.
the effect of colorectal cancer screening (CRC screening) on health behaviours, and the extent to which CRC screening can serve as a teachable health moment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FOBT is unlikely to be a teachable moment.
FOBT participation may not be a teachable moment, but may be a teachable opportunity.
FOBT participation may be a teachable moment, but only for a small number of behaviours.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FOBT participation is associated with some lifestyle changes but the effect is small.
the effect of cancer screening on multiple health behaviours is complex and may be context-dependent.
the effect of screening participation on multiple health behaviours may be limited.
The main takeaway from our work is that
screening programmes should consider the opportunity to provide advice and support for behaviour change, as part of their screening offer.
screening participation does not appear to be associated with a broad spectrum of lifestyle improvements, but it is possible that it may have a positive effect on vigorous physical activity.
there is little evidence to suggest that participation in FOBT is associated with lifestyle changes that are protective of future cancer risk.
